title: Epidemic threshold
text:
In applied surveillance, epidemic threshold is a statistical or operational cut-off separating “expected/endemic” from “excess/epidemic” counts.
there are two types of thresholds used to initiate response: an alert threshold and an epidemic threshold (WHO 2019)

Alert threshold: a lower cut-off whose, whose crossing triggers heightened vigilance, investigation and preparedness (but not yet full response). such as when there is one suspected case (as for an epidemic-prone disease or for a disease targeted for elimination or eradication) or when there is an unexplained increase for any disease or unusual pattern seen over a period of time in weekly or monthly summary reporting.
epidemic threshold: a higher cut-off whose crossing confirms epidemic activity and triggers control/response measures. For rare diseases or diseases targeted for eradication, detection of a single case suggests an epidemic. In such situations, one case is unusual and is a serious event. In other situations, a number of cases will trigger a response.

FOr example, alert threshold is 2nd quartile/Median of confirmed malaria cases for the past five years, epidemic threshold for malaria in some countries is 3rd Quartile of confirmed malaria cases (WHO 2019).
These threshold measure how deviation the current situation compared to a Endemic / baseline level: the expected, normal background frequency of a disease in a place/season (Disease Control and Prevention 2012).
This was first mentioned by Serfling “at a distance of 1.64 standard deviations above the trend line, a level which experience has shown to be useful for distinguishing epidemic increase from random variation.” (Serfling 1963). Observations above it indicate epidemic/excess activity. The Serfling approach remains the basis of CDC’s influenza epidemic threshold and excess-mortality estimation.

title: 1  CUSUM
text:
1.1 Computing an epidemic threshold with CUSUM
CUSUM adds up how far each reading strays from its target. Small shifts that no single reading would catch still pile up, so it spots a slow, steady change early, like the start of an outbreak. Click through the vaccine line in Figure 1.1: each vial is measured, and the CUSUM climbs until it signals.
E.S. Page invented CUSUM in 1954 for factory quality control (Page 1954). Tillett and Spencer brought it into disease surveillance in 1982, with weekly influenza “cusum graphs” for England and Wales (Tillett and Spencer 1982). Page tracked one parameter of a distribution, usually the mean, and set a rule for when a change was big enough to act on.
For weekly case counts, the standard tool is the CUSUM in R’s surveillance package (algo.cusum) (Rossi et al. 1999), building on counted-data CUSUMs (Lucas 1985). It runs in three steps, using the package defaults.
The defaults are \(k = 1.04\) and \(h = 2.26\), and \(S_t\) is not reset after a signal, so a whole outbreak stays flagged.
The same rule reads as a threshold on the raw count. To see where that threshold comes from, look at the accumulate step at the exact moment a week trips the alarm. At that point \(S_t = h\), and the running sum is positive, so the floor does nothing:
\[ h = S_{t-1} + (z_t - k). \]
Rearrange for the standardised deviation that just reaches the boundary:
\[ z_t = h + k - S_{t-1}. \]
Now put back \(z_t = (x_t - m)/\sqrt{m}\) from step 2:
\[ \frac{x_t - m}{\sqrt{m}} = h + k - S_{t-1}. \]
Multiply through by \(\sqrt{m}\) and add \(m\) to isolate the count:
\[ x_t = m + \sqrt{m}\,(h + k - S_{t-1}). \]
Cases are whole numbers, so the smallest count that reaches the boundary is this value rounded up. A week signals exactly when
\[ x_t \ge U_t = \left\lceil m + \sqrt{m}\,(h + k - S_{t-1}) \right\rceil, \]
the package’s upperbound. This \(U_t\) is the epidemic threshold in cases. It starts high and falls as evidence builds, so a steady rise is caught even when no single week looks extreme. Hover across Figure 1.2 to see each week’s numbers.

title: 1  CUSUM
text:
1. Expected level. Take the in-control mean \(m\), the count you expect in a normal week. By default the package uses the mean of the weeks before monitoring starts.


2. Standardise. Turn each count into a standardised deviation,
\[ z_t = \frac{x_t - m}{\sqrt{m}}, \]
so a normal week sits near \(z_t \approx 0\) whatever the size of \(m\).


3. Accumulate. Add up these deviations minus a reference value \(k\), floored at zero, and signal once the sum reaches the boundary \(h\):
\[ S_t = \max\!\left(0,\; S_{t-1} + (z_t - k)\right), \qquad \text{signal when } S_t \ge h. \]



















Figure 1.2: Simulated weekly cases. Weeks 1 to 13 set the expected count \(m = 8\). From week 14 the CUSUM \(S_t\) (bottom) builds up during the outbreak, and the case threshold \(U_t\) (red dashed step, top) falls as it does. Weeks that signal are red. Hover over or tap a week to see its numbers.

title: 2  RKI
text:
2.1 Computing an epidemic threshold with RKI
The RKI method asks a narrower question than a control chart does. Not “is this week high?”, but “is this week high for this week of the year?” It gathers a handful of comparable weeks — the same week in earlier years, and the weeks just gone — and treats what happened in them as what should happen now. It is the instinct behind judging a June electricity bill against last June rather than against the yearly average. Set the three parameters below and watch which weeks get pulled into the comparison.
The Robert Koch Institute built this into SurvNet, Germany’s national electronic notification system, in 2001 (Faensen et al. 2006; Robert Koch Institute, n.d.). It follows the CDC method of Stroup and colleagues (Stroup et al. 1989), which introduced the idea of judging a week against the equivalent weeks of earlier years rather than against one overall average. Höhle’s surveillance package implements it as algo.rki (Höhle 2007; Höhle and Riebler, n.d.).
For weekly case counts the tool is algo.rki in R’s surveillance package, with algo.rki1, algo.rki2 and algo.rki3 as named presets (Salmon et al. 2016). It runs in three steps.
The defaults are \(b=2\), \(w=4\) and actY = FALSE — the RKI 3 system — the comparison is strict, so a week that exactly meets the threshold stays quiet, and \(U_t\) is never rounded to a whole case, so 24 notifications against a threshold of 23.49 is a signal.

title: 2  RKI
text:
1. Reference set. Collect the weeks that count as comparable to week \(t\). They come from two places: a window of width \(2w+1\) centred on the equivalent week in each of the \(b\) previous years, and the \(w_0\) weeks immediately before \(t\) in the current year.
\[
R_{w,w_0,b} \;=\; \left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{b}\ \bigcup_{j=-w}^{w} y_{\,t-52i+j}\right)
\;\cup\; \left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{w_0} y_{\,t-k}\right)
\]
Here \(y_t\) is the number of cases notified in week \(t\), and 52 is the number of weeks the package assumes in a year.


2. Expected level. Average them.
\[ \hat\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{y \,\in\, R_{w,w_0,b}} y, \qquad n = \bigl|R_{w,w_0,b}\bigr|. \]
There is no fitted curve and no trend term. The reference weeks are the model.


3. Threshold. Take the upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval for a count of that size. algo.rki picks the interval two different ways, depending on how large \(\hat\mu\) is:
\[
U_t \;=\;
\begin{cases}
\hat\mu + 2\hat\sigma, & \hat\mu > 20,\\[4pt]
\tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975}\bigl(2(\lfloor\hat\mu\rfloor+1)\bigr), & \hat\mu \le 20,
\end{cases}
\]
with \(\hat\sigma\) the sample standard deviation of the reference values. A week signals when \(N_t > U_t\).



2.1.1 How many weeks the comparison uses
The two sources of reference weeks never overlap, provided \(w_0 < 52 - w\), so the size of the set is just the two pieces added together. Count each one.
The current year contributes a single week for each \(k\) from 1 to \(w_0\):
\[ n_{\text{current}} = w_0. \]
Each past year contributes a single week for each \(j\) from \(-w\) to \(w\), which is \(2w+1\) weeks, and there are \(b\) such years:
\[ n_{\text{past}} = b\,(2w+1). \]
Add them:
\[ n = w_0 + b\,(2w+1). \]
Nothing here depends on the case counts. The size of the comparison is fixed by the calendar alone, decided before any data is read, which is what makes the three published systems directly comparable.
One implementation detail matters when you go to run it. In algo.rki the two widths are not independent: the current-year window is switched on by actY and reuses the same \(w\), so
\[ w_0 = w \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\texttt{actY}\}, \]
and the package labels its output rki(w, w0, b) accordingly. A setting like \(w=1\) with \(w_0=2\) is expressible in the definition above but not through algo.rki; it needs a hand-rolled reference set.


2.1.2 Where the two branches come from
Both branches answer one question: how large can a count get before it stops looking like a draw from the reference level?
When the expected count is large, the reference values are roughly symmetric about their mean, and the upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval sits about two standard deviations above it. The package rounds 1.96 to 2 and takes
\[ U_t = \hat\mu + 2\hat\sigma. \]
When the expected count is small that approximation fails: counts are discrete, the distribution is skewed, and a symmetric interval can reach below zero. So the package uses the exact Poisson limit instead. For an observation \(x\), the upper limit is the rate at which \(x\) or fewer cases would be seen only 2.5% of the time:
\[ \Pr\bigl(X \le x \mid \lambda = U\bigr) = 0.025, \]
which has a closed form in terms of the chi-square quantile,
\[ U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975}\bigl(2(x+1)\bigr). \]
algo.rki reads this out of a stored table (CIdata, tabulated by Sachs (Sachs 1991)) at \(x = \lfloor\hat\mu\rfloor\), the reference mean rounded down to a whole case. That floor is why \(U_t\) is a step function: it holds still while the reference mean drifts, then jumps the moment the mean crosses an integer.
A quicker approximation is sometimes quoted for this step, \(\hat\mu +
1.96\sqrt{\hat\mu}\), which treats the reference mean as a Poisson rate. It lands close, but it is not what the package computes, and it is the more permissive of the two — on the example below it gives 23.16 where the table gives 24.74.


2.1.3 The example in Figure 2.1
The figure opens on a worked case. Week 25 of 2026 is assessed with \(b=3\), \(w=1\) and \(w_0=2\), so the reference set is the three weeks around week 25 in each of 2025, 2024 and 2023, plus weeks 23 and 24 of 2026 — eleven weeks in all, from the formula \(n = 2 + 3(2\cdot 1 + 1) = 11\). They average 15.45 cases. That is below 20, so the Poisson branch applies: \(\lfloor 15.45 \rfloor = 15\), and the table gives \(U = 24.74\). Twenty-one notifications would pass; twenty-six would signal.
Raising \(w_0\) pulls more of the current year into the comparison, and lowering it pushes the method back onto earlier years. That single trade is what separates the three published systems.

title: 2  RKI
text:
2.2 RKI 1, RKI 2 and RKI 3

RKI 1 — \(b=0\), \(w=6\), actY = TRUE, six reference weeks. The six weeks just gone, and nothing else. It has no memory of previous years, so it cannot know what time of year it is; what it can do is react within six weeks of a change.


RKI 2 — \(b=1\), \(w=6\), actY = TRUE, nineteen reference weeks. The same six recent weeks, plus the thirteen weeks centred on the equivalent week one year ago. Roughly half recent, half seasonal.


RKI 3 — \(b=2\), \(w=4\), actY = FALSE, eighteen reference weeks. The current year is dropped entirely; nine weeks are taken around the equivalent week in each of the two previous years. Every reference week is seasonal.







Figure 2.2: The same simulated series under all three systems. Hover a week to see the reference weeks behind it.



The consequence is visible in Figure 2.2. Because RKI 1 and RKI 2 include the weeks immediately before \(t\), a rise that lasts more than a few weeks enters its own reference set and lifts its own threshold behind it. The simulated rise in the fourth year of the figure spans weeks 14 to 25 of 2025: RKI 1 flags two of those weeks, RKI 2 flags four, and RKI 3 — which never looks at the current year — flags six.
That is not a ranking. It is a trade, and it runs in both directions. RKI 3 keeps a baseline no ongoing outbreak can inflate, but it cannot report at all until two full years of history exist behind it; in the figure it stays silent until week 5 of 2024, while RKI 1 is running by week 7 of 2022. A short memory buys speed and a short warm-up and pays for it in seasonal blindness. A long one buys a seasonal baseline and pays for it in start-up time and in slower recognition that the baseline itself has shifted.
The series in Figure 2.2 is simulated, not observed. It is there to show how the threshold behaves, not how dengue behaves.

title: 2  RKI
text:
2.3 Poisson or negative binomial
Every threshold so far has assumed that a week’s count varies about as much as its own average. That is what lets \(\sqrt{\hat\mu}\) carry the whole of step 3: Poisson counts have variance equal to their mean, so the mean alone fixes the spread, and no separate variance has to be estimated.
The choice between the two distributions is not a choice about which disease you are watching. It comes down to one question about the reference weeks: do they vary more than their own mean?
Poisson says no. It holds when cases arrive independently, at a rate that does not move across the reference weeks. Three things break that, and any one is enough:

Cases are not independent. One case produces others, so they arrive in lumps rather than one at a time.
The rate itself moves. Whatever drives transmission changes across the reference weeks, so they are not draws from a single distribution.
Reporting is uneven. A delayed week followed by a double week adds variance that has nothing to do with transmission.

All three inflate the variance and leave the mean alone — the one failure Poisson cannot express, because it has no parameter for it.

2.3.1 What it costs to get this wrong
Write the excess as a dispersion factor \(\varphi = \operatorname{Var}(y) /
\operatorname{E}(y)\), so \(\varphi = 1\) under Poisson. A negative binomial with mean \(\mu\) and dispersion \(\varphi\) has variance \(\varphi\mu\), so its standard deviation is
\[ \sqrt{\varphi\mu} \;=\; \sqrt{\varphi}\,\sqrt{\mu}. \]
The distance from the mean up to any quantile is a multiple of the standard deviation, so it widens by \(\sqrt{\varphi}\), not by \(\varphi\). Doubling the variance moves the threshold out by about 41%.
Small in the threshold, large in the alarm rate. The algo.rki Poisson branch starts out conservative — a confidence limit read from a table, not a predictive quantile — so on true Poisson counts it fires on about one normal week in a hundred, not the one in twenty its 95% label suggests. At \(\varphi = 3\), a threshold meant to fire on about 1% of normal weeks fires on 9%: a false alarm every eleven weeks in place of one every two years. In cases, the worked example’s threshold of 24.74 would have to sit at 33.
The error runs one way only. Assuming Poisson when \(\varphi > 1\) costs specificity, never sensitivity.


2.3.2 Choosing
\(\varphi\) is estimated, not assumed. Estimate it from a long stretch of non-epidemic weeks — not from the reference set, whose 18 or 19 values are far too few. The usual estimator is the Pearson dispersion of a quasi-Poisson fit with the seasonality left in:
fit <- glm(cases ~ t + sin(2*pi*week/52) + cos(2*pi*week/52),
           family = quasipoisson, data = baseline)
summary(fit)$dispersion
Near 1, stay with Poisson. algo.rki works as it stands, needs no second estimate, and a badly fitted dispersion is its own source of error.
Above about 2, move to the negative binomial. Table 2.1 applies, and the Poisson threshold is delivering several times the alarm rate it claims.
In between, prefer Poisson when the baseline is short. A \(\hat\varphi\) drawn from two years of weekly data is itself uncertain, and over-estimating it raises the threshold and hides outbreaks Poisson would have caught.
algo.rki has no negative binomial option. The smallest change keeps its reference set and replaces only the last step: a negative binomial with mean \(\hat\mu\) and variance \(\hat\varphi\hat\mu\) has size parameter \(k = \hat\mu / (\hat\varphi - 1)\), so
U <- qnbinom(1 - alpha, mu = mu_hat, size = mu_hat / (phi_hat - 1))
The reference weeks, the calendar and the decision rule are unchanged; only the tail is. Beyond that, farringtonFlexible estimates dispersion as part of fitting and downweights past outbreaks so they cannot inflate the baseline (Farrington et al. 1996; Noufaily et al. 2013), and boda fits a negative binomial outright (Salmon et al. 2016) — both at far more computation than RKI.

title: 3  Bayesian
text:
3.1 What a reference set leaves behind
Every method so far has answered “how high is too high” by looking up comparable weeks and asking how far above them this week sits. This one answers it differently. It writes down a full probability distribution for what next week’s count could be, then cuts that distribution at a high quantile and calls everything above the cut a signal.
The difference lives entirely in the tail. A distribution built from parameters you pretend to know is narrower than one built from parameters you admit you had to estimate, and a narrower distribution puts the threshold lower than it should be. Raise the uncertainty slider below and watch the two thresholds come apart.
The algorithm is BODA, the Bayesian Outbreak Detection Algorithm of Manitz and Höhle (Manitz and Höhle 2013), implemented in R’s surveillance package as boda() (Salmon et al. 2016). Salmon and colleagues later extended it to handle reporting delay (Salmon et al. 2015), which is bodaDelay().
Before the method, the complaint it answers. Reference-value methods — the CUSUM and RKI chapters both belong here — pay for their simplicity in four ways.
One clarification is worth making before going further, because the chapter title invites the wrong reading. The line that separates these two families is not frequentist against Bayesian. It is reference values against a regression model. The Bayesian framework by itself fixes only the third complaint, the plug-in step. The other three fall only because the method moves to a full regression on the whole series.
The package makes the point for you. surveillance also ships algo.bayes, which is Bayesian and still reference-value based — and still has all three of the other problems.

title: 3  Bayesian
text:
They use a sliver of the data. A handful of weeks from a handful of years decides the threshold. The rest of the series still carries information about trend and seasonality, and none of it is read.


The answer depends on a window you chose. How many years back, how many weeks either side. Section 2.1.1 showed those choices fixing the size of the comparison before any data is read, and nothing in the method tells you which choice is right.


They act as though the estimate were the truth. The reference mean is substituted straight into the predictive distribution, as if it were known rather than estimated. This is the plug-in step, and it is what narrows the distribution and drops the threshold.


There is nowhere to put a cause. Cases rise for reasons — weather, population movement, a change in who gets tested. A reference set has no slot for any of them.

title: 3  Bayesian
section: 3.2 Computing an epidemic threshold with BODA
text:
3.2 Computing an epidemic threshold with BODA
boda() runs in six steps. The first three build a model, the fourth fits it, and the last two turn the fit into a number you can compare a count against.

1. Choose the distribution. Case counts almost always vary more than their own mean, because transmission clusters and so the observations are not independent. Section 2.3 made that case in full; BODA takes it as the starting point and uses a negative binomial throughout:
\[ y_t \mid \mu_t, \nu \;\sim\; \mathrm{NB}(\mu_t, \nu), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_t) = \mu_t + \frac{\mu_t^2}{\nu}. \]
Watch the direction of \(\nu\), which is easy to read backwards. A larger \(\nu\) means less spread; as \(\nu \to \infty\) the distribution collapses to Poisson. It measures the inverse of overdispersion.


2. Model the expected count. Everything that should move the expectation goes into a linear predictor on the log scale:
\[ \log \mu_t \;=\; \log P_t + \alpha_{0t} + \beta t + \gamma_t + X_t^{\!\top}\delta + \zeta z_t. \]
Each term has one job. \(\log P_t\) is a population offset, so the model works on rates rather than raw counts and districts of different sizes can be compared. \(\alpha_{0t}\) is an intercept free to drift, smoothing the baseline level. \(\beta t\) is long-run trend. \(\gamma_t\) is the seasonal cycle, period 52 for weekly data. \(X_t^{\!\top}\delta\) is where covariates enter — temperature, absolute humidity, rainfall, usually lagged. And \(\zeta z_t\) marks weeks already flagged as aberrant, so that old epidemic peaks are not learned as ordinary baseline.

That last term deserves a second look, because it sounds like the objection raised against reference methods: doesn’t somebody have to decide in advance which weeks were epidemic? No. In the implementation z_t is not supplied by the user. With pastAberrations = TRUE, it is read from the alarms the algorithm itself raised at earlier time points. The loop closes on its own.

3. Put a prior on everything. In a Bayesian model every parameter is a random variable and needs a distribution before the data arrives. This model is a latent Gaussian model, which splits the parameters into two tiers: a latent field \(x = (\alpha_{0t}, \beta, \gamma_t, \delta, \zeta)\) of regression coefficients and random effects, assumed jointly Gaussian; and a small set of hyperparameters \(\theta = (\nu, \tau)\) controlling dispersion and how smooth each effect is.
The split is not bookkeeping. Keeping the hyperparameters few — under about fifteen — is the condition that makes step 4 possible (Rue et al. 2009).

In practice: the drifting intercept is declared through f(time, model = ...), where rw1 (a first-order random walk, a slowly wandering baseline) is a sensible default for weekly data, with iid and rw2 as the looser and smoother alternatives. Setting season = TRUE gives the seasonal term a cyclic spline, so the end of one year joins the start of the next. Fixed coefficients get vague Gaussian priors and let the data speak. For the hyperparameters INLA defaults to log-Gamma; on short series or thin ward-level counts, a PC prior is less sensitive to how you set it. Run the whole thing under at least two prior choices and check the answer does not move.

4. Fit it. With weeks \(1\) to \(T-1\) in hand, Bayes’ theorem gives
\[ p(x, \theta \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;\propto\; p(y_{1:T-1} \mid x, \theta)\, p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta). \]
The normalising constant is an integral with no closed form. MCMC would sample it accurately and take hours for one series — impossible for a system that runs weekly across hundreds of units. BODA uses INLA instead (Rue et al. 2009), a deterministic approximation built for exactly this class of model, which matches MCMC closely and runs orders of magnitude faster.


5. Average over what you do not know. The parameters were never the point. What is wanted is \(y_T\), and the distribution for it integrates the model away:
\[ p(y_T \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;=\; \int p(y_T \mid x, \theta)\, p(x, \theta \mid y_{1:T-1})\, \mathrm{d}x\, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]
This single line is the whole argument of the chapter. It folds together two different uncertainties: counts bounce around even when the parameters are known exactly, and the parameters are not known exactly. Plug-in methods carry only the first.

One implementation detail follows directly from step 4 and is easy to get wrong. INLA returns the marginal posterior of each parameter, not their joint distribution. boda() therefore takes a samplingMethod argument, and it should be set to 'joint'. Sampling each marginal independently discards the correlations between parameters and narrows the predictive distribution — reintroducing, by the back door, the exact defect the method exists to remove.

6. Cut the tail. The threshold is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of that predictive distribution. Counts are whole numbers, so the honest definition is the smallest integer whose cumulative probability reaches \(1-\alpha\):
\[ \xi_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \min\Bigl\{ k \in \{0,1,2,\dots\} \;:\; \textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k} p(y_T = j \mid y_{1:T-1}) \;\ge\; 1-\alpha \Bigr\}. \]
A week signals when \(y_T^{\text{obs}} > \xi_{1-\alpha}\).


3.2.1 Why the Bayesian threshold sits higher
The claim that the predictive distribution is wider can be made exact. Split its variance by conditioning on the parameters first:
\[ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \operatorname{E}\!\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \mu)\bigr] \;+\; \operatorname{Var}\!\bigl(\operatorname{E}[y_T \mid \mu]\bigr). \]
The first term is how much the counts would scatter if you knew where they were centred. The second is how much the centre itself could move.
Substitute the negative binomial, for which \(\operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mu) = \mu +
\mu^2/\nu\) and \(\operatorname{E}[y \mid \mu] = \mu\):
\[ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \operatorname{E}[\mu] + \frac{\operatorname{E}[\mu^2]}{\nu} + \operatorname{Var}(\mu). \]
Write \(\hat\mu = \operatorname{E}[\mu]\) and \(s^2 = \operatorname{Var}(\mu)\), and use \(\operatorname{E}[\mu^2] = \hat\mu^2 + s^2\):
\[ \operatorname{Var}(y_T \mid \text{data}) \;=\; \underbrace{\hat\mu + \frac{\hat\mu^2}{\nu}}_{\text{plug-in}} \;+\; s^2\Bigl(1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\Bigr). \]
The brace is exactly what a plug-in method computes. Everything after it is what a plug-in method discards, and it has a shape worth reading. The penalty grows with the square of how uncertain the expected count is, so it stays negligible until the estimate is genuinely shaky and then grows fast. And it is larger when \(\nu\) is small: the more overdispersed the counts already are, the more parameter uncertainty piles on top.
Figure 3.1 opens at \(\hat\mu = 15\), \(\nu = 6\) and 30% uncertainty. The plug-in variance is 52.50, the formula adds about 24.7, and the total is 77.17. In cases, the plug-in threshold is 28 and the Bayesian one is 32 — and a threshold of 28 that advertises a 5% false alarm rate delivers 7.6%.

title: 3  Bayesian
section: 3.3 When this week’s count is not yet this week’s count
text:
3.3 When this week’s count is not yet this week’s count
For ward-level surveillance this is not a refinement. It is the main problem.
A week’s count is never finished when the week is. Cases have to present, be tested, be confirmed and be entered, and all of that takes time. So at the moment the algorithm runs, the current week is under-reported — while the threshold it is compared against was calibrated on historical weeks that have long since filled in. The comparison is between an incomplete number and a complete-number threshold, and it fails in the worst possible direction: outbreaks are missed precisely when detecting them matters most.






Figure 3.2: The same forty weeks under two rules. Hollow outlines are the counts once every case has arrived; solid bars are what is visible when the week is judged. Rings mark exceedances the rule fails to see.



Set the wait to zero and read the figure as reported: only about a third of each week’s cases exist yet, and all three genuine exceedances slip under the threshold. Wait two weeks and all three are caught — but every alarm now arrives two weeks after the week it describes, which for a vector-borne outbreak is most of the window in which a response would have helped.
The second tab is the way out. If you know what share of a week’s cases has usually arrived by a given delay, you can scale the partial count back up and judge the week immediately. That is what delay correction does, and at a wait of zero it recovers all three.
Salmon and colleagues built this into the model rather than bolting it on (Salmon et al. 2015). The data are treated as a two-way table — week of onset against reporting delay — with the lower right corner missing, and that table is modelled with negative binomial regression. The implementation is bodaDelay(), and using it means preparing a reporting triangle rather than a plain weekly series.
Worth knowing before you plan around it: bodaDelay() combines the Manitz–Höhle algorithm with Noufaily’s (Noufaily et al. 2013), and so it still takes reference-window arguments b and w. The dependence on a chosen window, the second complaint in Section 3.1, is therefore not fully removed. That is a deliberate trade of theoretical tidiness for something that runs.

title: 3  Bayesian
text:
3.4 Practical notes
The software is experimental. boda() says so in its own documentation. It depends on INLA, which is not on CRAN and installs from its own repository:
install.packages("INLA", repos = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable")
It is slow, because a Bayesian model is fitted at every time point. And results are not reproducible under INLA’s default parallelism; for a reproducible run, set INLA::inla.setOption(num.threads = "1:1") before set.seed().
Many units at once is a different problem. This is the easiest thing to overlook when moving from one series to a whole city. Run the algorithm across \(N\) units at level \(\alpha\) and, with no outbreak anywhere, the expected number of false alarms per week is \(N\alpha\). For 168 units at \(\alpha = 0.05\) that is about eight false alarms every week — enough to exhaust a response team’s trust within a few months. The options are to lower \(\alpha\) and accept the loss of sensitivity, to control a false discovery rate rather than each alarm separately, or to require a signal to repeat across weeks or cluster in space before it triggers fieldwork. Whichever you pick, write down why.
Use the population offset. When units differ greatly in size, \(\log P_t\) has to enter the model as an offset. Without it, dense wards carry permanently high thresholds and sparse ones alarm constantly, and neither reflects real risk. Check whether the version of boda() you are running accepts an offset, since its X argument takes covariates as fixed effects only.

title: 3  Bayesian
text:
3.5 Measuring whether it works
A detection algorithm is worth only what it can be shown to do. The minimum set: sensitivity (the share of real outbreaks detected), specificity and the false alarm rate, and timeliness — an algorithm that detects everything four weeks late detects nothing useful. Because the output here is a whole distribution rather than a yes-or-no verdict, add a proper scoring rule, which grades the probability forecast itself.
Evaluate on both simulated data, where the true outbreaks are known by construction, and on real historical series, which is how Manitz and Höhle assessed BODA (Manitz and Höhle 2013). Unkel and colleagues give a fuller comparison framework (Unkel et al. 2012).

title: 4  Farrington
text:
4.1 Computing an epidemic threshold with Farrington
Farrington asks the same question as RKI: is this week high for this time of year? RKI averages comparable weeks from past years. Farrington fits a regression line through them instead, so the expected count can follow a trend, and the scatter of ordinary weeks is measured, not assumed. It was built in England and Wales to screen weekly laboratory reports (Farrington et al. 1996), and Salmon et al. (2016) call it the method of choice at European public health institutes.
The method runs in four steps, and each one has a figure to play with.

title: 4  Farrington
text:
4.1.1 Step 1: choose comparable weeks
Counts rise and fall with the seasons, so this week is compared only with the same time of year in past years. If this is week \(x\) of year \(y\), the baseline is weeks \(x-w\) to \(x+w\) of the years \(y-b\) to \(y-1\): \(b\) years back, \(w\) weeks either side. That gives
\[ n = b\,(2w+1) \]
baseline weeks. Farrington and colleagues used \(b = 5\) and \(w = 3\), so \(n = 35\).






Figure 4.1: The baseline for week 25 of 2026. Each row is one year of weekly counts, and the teal bars are the baseline weeks. Change \(b\) and \(w\). The counts are simulated.



This choice of weeks is how the method handles seasonality, so the model needs no seasonal term. A wider window, or more years, gives more weeks to learn from. But a wide window reaches into another part of the season, and old years may reflect old reporting habits or laboratory methods (Farrington et al. 1996). The current year is never used, so an outbreak in progress cannot raise its own baseline.


4.1.2 Step 2: fit a line through the windows
Each baseline count \(y_i\), in week \(t_i\), has mean \(\mu_i\) and variance \(\varphi\mu_i\). This is a quasi-Poisson model: a Poisson model in which the variance may be larger than the mean. The only systematic effect is a straight-line trend on the log scale:
\[ \log \mu_i = \alpha + \beta\, t_i. \]
Weeks are counted from the first baseline week, so the baseline weeks are \(t = 1\) to \(7\), \(53\) to \(59\), and so on, and this week is \(t_0 = 264\). The line carried forward to \(t_0\) gives the expected count, \(\hat\mu_0 = \exp(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta\, t_0)\). The scatter around the line gives the dispersion, with Poisson scatter as the floor (Section 2.3):
\[ \hat\varphi = \max\left\{1,\ \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_i\,
\frac{(y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2}{\hat\mu_i}\right\}, \]
where \(p\) is 2 with the trend and 1 without. Every weight \(\omega_i\) is 1 until step 4.






Figure 4.2: The 35 baseline weeks of Figure 4.1 on the time axis, with the fitted line carried forward to this week. Drag a year up or down: the line, \(\hat\varphi\) and the three trend checks update. The red dashed mark is the threshold \(U\) from step 3.



The trend is kept only if all three checks pass (Farrington et al. 1996):

the baseline spans at least 3 years;
\(\beta\) is significant at the 5% level;
\(\hat\mu_0\) is no larger than the largest baseline count.

The third check stops a steep line from running away when it is carried a year past the data. If any check fails, the model is fitted again as a flat line.


4.1.3 Step 3: set the threshold
The threshold \(U\) is the top of a prediction interval: the range this week’s count should fall in if nothing unusual is happening. It allows for the scatter of the count (\(\hat\varphi\hat\mu_0\)) and for the uncertainty in \(\hat\mu_0\). It is built on the \(2/3\) power scale, where counts are close to symmetric:
\[ U = \hat\mu_0\left(1 + \frac{2}{3}\, z\,
\sqrt{\frac{\hat\varphi\hat\mu_0 + \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_0)}{\hat\mu_0^{2}}}\,\right)^{3/2}. \]
By default farrington() uses \(z = 1.96\), the top of a two-sided 95% interval (Salmon et al. 2016). The week raises an alarm when its count is above \(U\), unless fewer than 5 cases were reported in the last 4 weeks (Farrington et al. 1996).


4.1.4 Step 4: discount old outbreaks
An old outbreak in the baseline pulls the line up and inflates \(\hat\varphi\), so the threshold rises and the next outbreak is harder to see. Farrington therefore fits the model again, with less weight on weeks far above the line. Each week gets a standardised residual \(s_i\) (an Anscombe residual: its distance from the line on the \(2/3\) power scale, divided by its standard deviation), and
\[
\omega_i =
\begin{cases}
\gamma\, s_i^{-2}, & s_i > c,\\
\gamma, & s_i \le c,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\gamma\) makes the weights add up to \(n\). Only weeks above the line can lose weight. In the package, this refit comes straight after the first fit, before the trend checks and the threshold.






Figure 4.3: The baseline of Figure 4.2 with an outbreak added to 2023. Hollow circles have lost weight, and the paler the circle, the smaller its weight. The grey dashed line is the fit with every week at full weight. Hover over or tap a circle to see \(s_i\) and its weight.



The cut-off \(c\) decides how much of the past is believed. For ordinary weeks \(s_i\) is roughly standard normal, so the 1996 cut-off \(c = 1\) also shrinks about 1 ordinary week in 6. Those weeks carry the ordinary scatter, so \(\hat\varphi\) and the threshold fall: choose No outbreak and c = 1 to see it. Noufaily et al. (2013) raised the cut-off to \(c = 2.58\), which touches about 1 ordinary week in 200. In a 35-week baseline, though, 2.58 can miss much of an old outbreak: the outbreak inflates \(\hat\varphi\), and a larger \(\hat\varphi\) shrinks every residual, including its own. Noufaily and colleagues paired the higher cut-off with a much longer baseline.

title: 4  Farrington
text:
4.3 Running it in R
Both versions are in R’s surveillance package (Salmon et al. 2016).
library(tidyverse)
library(surveillance)

# weekly: one row per week, with columns date (a Date) and cases
cases <- sts(observed = weekly$cases, epoch = weekly$date, frequency = 52)

res96 <- cases |> farrington(control = list(b = 5, w = 3, alpha = 0.05))

res13 <- cases |> farringtonFlexible(control = list(
  b = 5, w = 3,
  noPeriods = 10,               # 10-level seasonal factor
  pastWeeksNotIncluded = 26,
  pThresholdTrend = 1,          # no significance test for the trend
  weightsThreshold = 2.58,
  thresholdMethod = "nbPlugin",
  alpha = 0.05                  # one-sided in this function
))

autoplot(res13)                 # counts, threshold and alarms (ggplot2)
Two things catch people out:

alpha is two-sided in farrington() but one-sided in farringtonFlexible(), so the same value gives a lower threshold, and more alarms, in the newer function.
The defaults of farringtonFlexible() are neither version: the 1996 baseline, trend test and threshold, with the 2013 cut-off of 2.58. A misspelled name in control is ignored without a warning, so copy the names exactly.

title: 4  Farrington
text:
4.4 What an alarm means
An alarm means this week’s count is higher than the model predicted for this time of year, at the chosen error rate. It is a prompt to check, not a confirmed outbreak: at a one-sided 5% level, 100 series give about 5 chance alarms every week. The design also has limits:

It judges each week alone, so a slow, sustained rise can slip through. CUSUM adds up that evidence.
It assumes the season comes at the same time every year. An early or late season is compared with the wrong weeks.
It has no place for covariates (other drivers of the counts, such as rainfall). BODA adds them (Section 3.2).

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
5.1 The method in brief
The Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) sets thresholds for weekly influenza-like illness (ILI) or acute respiratory infection (ARI) rates from past seasons (Vega et al. 2013). This chapter follows its steps one by one, with a figure for each step. The data are weekly ILI consultation rates per 100,000 in Croatia, week 26 of 2022 to week 43 of 2026, from ECDC’s European Respiratory Virus Surveillance Summary (ERVISS) (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control 2026). In each figure, point at a blue symbol in a formula to see where it is in the chart.
MEM uses past seasons to set thresholds for the next season. It works in three steps.
In a new season, the first weekly rate above the epidemic threshold signals the start of the epidemic. The intensity thresholds then give the level of each week.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
Find the epidemic weeks. For each past season, the MAP curve gives the length and the timing of the epidemic. This splits the season into three periods: pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic.
Set the epidemic threshold. From each pre-epidemic period, take the \(n\) highest weekly rates, where \(n = 30 / \text{number of seasons}\). Pool these values from all seasons. The epidemic threshold is their mean plus \(z_{0.05}\) standard deviations, where \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\). A post-epidemic threshold comes from the post-epidemic periods in the same way.
Set the intensity thresholds. From each epidemic period, take the \(n\) highest weekly rates and pool them. Their geometric mean and upper limits give the thresholds for the levels of intensity.



The purpose of the MEM is to model influenza epidemics based upon historical data from a specific country or region. The method has three main steps: First, the length, start and the end of the annual epidemics are determined, splitting the season in three periods: a pre-epidemic, an epidemic and a post-epidemic period. Secondly, the baseline and the epidemic thresholds are calculated using the pre-epidemic and post-epidemic values of historical seasons. Finally, thresholds for different levels of intensity are computed. (Vega et al. 2013)

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
section: 5.2 The data: one row per season
text:
5.2 The data: one row per season

Weekly rates were estimated at least for 33 weeks in every season, from week 40 of 1 year to the week 20 of the following year. (Vega et al. 2013)


Missing values in weekly rates at the beginning or at the end of the surveillance period did not affect the method and were excluded from calculations. Missing weekly data during the surveillance period were imputed with a smooth regression over the full season’s data using a small window parameter. (Vega et al. 2013)

A real series needs this preparation. Some weeks were never reported, some weeks fall between seasons, and the current season is not finished. The paper used countries with five or more seasons of data (Vega et al. 2013). ERVISS has four complete seasons for Croatia, so the numbers in this chapter are a worked example, not Croatia’s official thresholds.






Figure 5.1: Weekly ILI rates in Croatia as reported to ERVISS. Hatching marks weeks with no data; a week with no data is not a week with zero cases. Brackets mark the four complete seasons. Press Cut into seasons: the weeks between seasons and the unfinished current season are left out. One week inside a season has no data, week 19 of 2025. It is filled with a smoothing regression over the season, as in the authors’ R package (Lozano 2025); the regression gives a value below 0, so the week is set to 0.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
section: 5.3 Step 1: the epidemic period of each season
text:
5.3 Step 1: the epidemic period of each season

In the first step, for each season separately, the length of the epidemic period is estimated as the minimum number of consecutive weeks with the maximum accumulated rates percentage (MAP). (Vega et al. 2013)


The MAP curve draws the maximum cumulated rate for a period of a given length \(r\), expressed as percentage of the total rate of the \(j\)th season. (Vega et al. 2013)







Figure 5.2: The best window of \(r\) weeks in every season, beside the MAP curves. For each number of weeks \(r\), the window of \(r\) consecutive weeks is placed where its total is largest, so it can be in a different place in each season.




Then the MAP curve is smoothed, using a smoothing regression (over \(r\)), selecting automatically the window parameter. The optimum number of weeks for each season is determined calculating the increment in the percentage from one number of weeks to the next one. … When this increment is lower than the predefined criteria, the optimum is found. (Vega et al. 2013)

The criterion is \(\delta\). It depends on the country, ranges from 2% to 4% and is chosen to maximise sensitivity and specificity (Vega et al. 2013). Once the optimum number of weeks \(r^*\) is found, the epidemic starts at week \(k^*\), the first week of the window of \(r^*\) weeks with the largest total. The weeks before the epidemic are the pre-epidemic period, and the weeks after it are the post-epidemic period (Vega et al. 2013).






Figure 5.3: Left: the MAP curve of one season and its smoothed version. Right: the increment in the percentage from one number of weeks to the next. When the increment is lower than \(\delta\), the optimum length \(r^*\) is found. Bottom: the best window of \(r^*\) weeks starts at week \(k^*\); the epidemic runs from week \(k^*\) to week \(k^* + r^* - 1\), and this splits every season into three periods.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
5.4 Step 2: the epidemic threshold

In the second step, the baseline and threshold using pre-epidemic values of historical seasons are calculated. The baseline is the arithmetic mean of all pre-epidemic rates of all historical seasons (pooled together as a single sample). (Vega et al. 2013)


To calculate the threshold, only a set of pre-epidemic values is considered. For each season, the highest \(n\) values from the pre-epidemic period are taken, where \(n\) = 30/number of seasons. (Vega et al. 2013)


With all these \(n \times N\) values, a one-tailed point 95% confidence interval is calculated. … The upper limit of the confidence interval is the epidemic threshold. Additionally, a post-epidemic threshold is calculated using the same procedure. (Vega et al. 2013)

So the epidemic threshold is \(t^* = \bar{t} + z_{0.05} \times S_t\), where \(\bar{t}\) and \(S_t\) are the mean and the standard deviation of the \(n \times N\) values, and \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\). With four seasons, \(n = 30 / 4 = 7.5\), which the authors’ R package rounds to 8 (Lozano 2025), so 32 values are pooled.






NoteWhat is \(z_{0.05}\)?



95%5%meanmean + z0.05 SD
\(z_{0.05}\) is the point of the standard normal curve with 5% of the area above it. Its value is 1.645.
The calculation assumes that the pooled values come from a normal distribution with their mean and standard deviation. In any normal distribution, 95% of the values lie below the mean plus \(z_{0.05}\) standard deviations, and 5% lie above it.
The interval is one-tailed because only high rates matter for an alarm, so all of the 5% is in the upper tail. A two-tailed 95% interval would put 2.5% in each tail and use \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\) instead.
The interval is a point interval: it is for one weekly value, not for the mean. So it uses the standard deviation, not the standard error. In plain words, if the highest pre-epidemic weeks of a new season follow the same distribution as in past seasons, about 1 in 20 of them would still be above the threshold.








Figure 5.4: Top: every season, zoomed in on its pre-epidemic weeks; its \(n\) highest weeks are dark teal, with their rates per 100,000. Bottom left: the same \(n \times N\) values side by side. Bottom right: their histogram on its side, so that it shares the rate axis with the bars, with the normal curve of the same mean, standard deviation and area. The \(z\) axis on the right counts standard deviations from the mean. The threshold \(t^*\) is one horizontal line across both panels, at \(z_{0.05}\) on the \(z\) axis, with 5% of the curve’s area above it. Press Show how to watch the steps in order, and t* on the seasons to draw the threshold on every season.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
5.5 Step 3: the intensity thresholds

Thresholds for different levels of intensity are calculated using the \(n\) highest values of each epidemic period to build a sample of \(n \times N\) rates. With the sample, the geometric mean and 50%, 90% and 95% one-sided confidence intervals are calculated. These upper limits are the threshold for the different levels of intensity of the epidemic. (Vega et al. 2013)

As in step 2, \(z_\alpha\) is the point of the standard normal curve with \(\alpha\) of the area above it. Step 3 uses it on the logarithms of the rates: \(z_{0.50} = 0\) for the 50% limit, which is the geometric mean itself, \(z_{0.10} = 1.282\) for the 90% limit and \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\) for the 95% limit. The three thresholds split the weekly rates into five levels: baseline, low, medium, high and very high (Vega et al. 2015). The paper says countries may change these percentages (Vega et al. 2013). Vega et al. (2015) and the authors’ R package (Lozano 2025) use 40%, 90% and 97.5%.






Figure 5.5: Top: every season, zoomed in on its epidemic weeks; its \(n\) highest weeks are dark blue, with their rates. Bottom: the same values side by side, and their histogram on its side, on a log axis. The normal curve of the logs is centred on the geometric mean (\(z = 0\)); the 90% and 95% limits are at \(z_{0.10}\) and \(z_{0.05}\) on the \(z\) axis. So the three thresholds split the curve’s area into 50%, 40%, 5% and 5%. Switch to the rate scale to see the same values and the same curve on the rates. Press I50, I90, I95 on the seasons to draw the thresholds on every season.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
5.6 Step 4: watching a new season

The main purpose of the method is to define the baseline influenza activity in historical data and to establish an epidemic threshold above which the weekly rates are considered to be in the epidemic period. (Vega et al. 2013)


Rates in the pre-epidemic period were expected to be lower than the pre-epidemic threshold rate, while rates within the epidemic period are expected to be higher. Finally, rates in the post-epidemic period were expected to be lower than the post-epidemic threshold rate. (Vega et al. 2013)

The paper calls the first week with a rate above the epidemic threshold the alert week (Vega et al. 2013). During the epidemic, the intensity thresholds give the level of each week. The paper gives no rule for the end of the epidemic in a new season; the authors’ R package ends it at the first week after the peak with a rate below the post-epidemic threshold (Lozano 2025).

If influenza weekly epidemiological data are accompanied by timely virological data, virus circulation should be taken into account to make appropriate public health decisions. (Vega et al. 2013)

Figure 5.6 starts with the current season, 2026/27, and the thresholds from all four past seasons. The data end in week 43 of 2026. To show how a season reaches the threshold, the weeks after that are illustrative, not data: each one is the average rate of the four past seasons in the same week.






Figure 5.6: Press Play to add the weeks one by one. Solid bars are data and outlined bars are illustrative; the colour of a bar gives its level. At the right, step 3’s curve of past epidemic weeks stands on its side, cut at the intensity thresholds. Choose a past season to replay it, as in the paper’s cross-validation below.




For each country, each single season was extracted from the historical records to be used as the target season. MEM calculated the beginning and the end of the epidemic period of the target season. On the basis of the remaining seasons, excluding the target season, MEM calculated the pre- and post-epidemic thresholds. (Vega et al. 2013)

In a replay, the band under the chart is the epidemic period that step 1 finds for the target season, and the reading scores the alert with the paper’s timeliness, detection lag and false alerts.

title: 5  Moving Epidemic Method
text:
5.7 Notes

The paper gives step 3 in words. The formulas in Figure 5.5 are how the authors’ R package computes it (Lozano 2025).
The MAP curve is smoothed by a local linear kernel regression with the window chosen by AICc. The results were checked against R’s sm package.
The data are the ERVISS snapshot of 30 October 2026, released under the EUPL 1.2 licence (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control 2026).

title: 6  Serfling
text:
6.1 Overview
Every method so far has asked whether this week is unusual for this time of year. The Farrington chapter ended on a question that kind of method cannot answer — has the epidemic season started? — because a normal seasonal rise is, by construction, not unusual for its time of year. Serfling’s method models what the year would look like with no epidemic in it, and treats anything well above that line as epidemic activity. Like a tide table, which predicts the water level from a few regular cycles so that a storm surge is whatever it did not predict, Serfling’s baseline is a slow trend plus a few waves of fixed length, fitted to years with the epidemics taken out.
Robert E. Serfling published the method in 1963 at the US Communicable Disease Center (CDC), to monitor weekly deaths from pneumonia and influenza (P&I) in 108 US cities (Serfling 1963). He chose P&I deaths although they lag influenza cases by about four weeks, because case reports and school or work absences were not quantitative enough or not available widely. A parametric periodic regression model, it remains sixty years on one of the foundations of epidemic thresholds (Unkel et al. 2012).
For a seasonal disease one fixed threshold does not work: low enough to catch an epidemic outside the season, it fires all through the peak season; high enough for the peak season, it misses epidemics outside it. Serfling lets the threshold move with the seasonal baseline.

title: 6  Serfling
text:
NoteCore idea



Epidemic threshold = the expected level with no epidemic + a safety margin for random variation. The variants of Serfling differ mainly in how they estimate these two components.

title: 6  Serfling
text:
6.2 The procedure at a glance
The method rests on three ideas: a baseline built from a long-term trend and sine and cosine waves (a Fourier series); training data cleaned of past epidemics, so that they do not pull the baseline up; and a threshold a margin above the baseline, usually 1.64–1.645 standard deviations of the error, that must be crossed two weeks in a row (Serfling 1963). In practice that is four steps (Figure 6.1). Section 6.3 builds the model behind step 2; Section 6.4 details each step and works through all four on one data set.






Figure 6.1: Serfling’s procedure on simulated weekly data. Click a step to read it in full.

title: 6  Serfling
text:
6.3 Mathematical basis

6.3.1 The general equation
The Serfling model with \(r\) harmonics has the form (Serfling 1963):
\[
E\left(Y_t\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{i=1}^{r}\left[\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right)\right]
\tag{6.1}\]



Table 6.1: Symbols in the Serfling equation.









Symbol
Meaning




\(Y_t\)
Observed value of the surveillance indicator at time \(t\) (cases, deaths, a percentage…)


\(t\)
Continuous time index, \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, n\)


\(\beta_0\)
Intercept: the mean baseline level at the time origin


\(\beta_1\)
Long-term (secular) trend coefficient, reflecting changes in population or in the reporting system


\(L\)
Length of one annual cycle: 52 for weekly data, 13 for four-week periods (as in the original paper), 12 for monthly data


\(r\)
Number of harmonics included in the model


\(\gamma_i,\ \delta_i\)
Coefficients of the cosine and sine waves of harmonic \(i\)






Each parameter has one job (Figure 6.2): \(\beta_0\) sets the level, \(\beta_1\) tilts the curve from year to year, and each pair \(\gamma_i,\ \delta_i\) sets how tall one seasonal wave is and when it peaks. The trend can also be quadratic or cubic when the data change nonlinearly (Pelat et al. 2007). Serfling wrote the equation as \(\hat{Y} = u + bt + \sum a_i\cos\theta + \sum b_i\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) linear in \(t\) (Serfling 1963); this lesson uses \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) to avoid clashing with later notation.






Figure 6.2: Equation 6.1 over three years of weekly data (\(L = 52\)): the dotted line is the trend, the blue curve adds the seasonal waves. The starting values are the true baseline of the data in Section 6.4.1.





6.3.2 Fourier series, intuitively
Any curve that repeats every year can be assembled from sine and cosine waves of different frequencies, as a chord is built from single notes. Harmonic 1 has period \(L\) (52 weeks) and rises and falls once a year; harmonic 2 has period \(L/2\) (26 weeks) and rises and falls twice; harmonic \(i\) rises and falls \(i\) times. At each harmonic, the cosine–sine pair is one wave with an amplitude and a phase:
\[
\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) = A_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L} - \theta_i\right),\qquad A_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i^2 + \delta_i^2}
\]
\(A_i\) is how tall the wave is and \(\theta_i\) when it peaks. The cosine alone peaks at the start of the cycle, the sine alone a quarter of a cycle later; mixing them in the ratio \(\gamma_i : \delta_i\) puts the peak in any week. And because \(\gamma_i\) and \(\delta_i\) enter the model linearly, ordinary linear regression estimates them; no nonlinear fit of the phase is needed. The analyst chooses only \(L\) and \(r\): the frequencies are fixed, and the data decide how tall each wave is and where it peaks.
Figure 6.3 lets you do the regression’s job by hand: set the four coefficients until your curve runs through a year of weekly data, then compare with least squares, which makes the squared distances as small as possible.






Figure 6.3: Fitting a Fourier series by hand. Amber lines are the distances from each week to your curve. A symmetric peak needs only harmonic 1; a lopsided peak, or two peaks a year, also needs harmonic 2.



The first-order model (\(r = 1\)) gives exactly one symmetric peak a year:
\[
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \varepsilon_t
\]
The second-order model (\(r = 2\)) adds a semi-annual wave, allowing two peaks a year or one asymmetric peak that rises fast and falls slowly:
\[
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \gamma_2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \delta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \varepsilon_t
\]
A larger \(r\) follows more complex shapes, but pushed too far the model fits random noise and leftover epidemic peaks as well. So \(r\) is chosen by a statistical test, not by eye.


6.3.3 Choosing the number of harmonics: the example in the original paper
Serfling fitted the model to P&I deaths in 108 US cities over three seasons without a major epidemic (leaving out the 1957–58 pandemic), in thirteen four-week periods a year (Serfling 1963). To decide on a second harmonic he used Bliss’s analysis of variance, a partial F test: the variance added by harmonic 2 (mean square 8,136) was smaller than the residual variance of the second-order model (13,157), so \(F \approx 0.62 < 1\). Harmonic 2 explained no more than noise, and the first-order model was kept:
\[
\hat{Y}_t = 300.5 + 2.1\, t + 97.6\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{13} - 2.67\right)
\tag{6.2}\]
Here \(t\) is in four-week periods, from the midpoint of the period ending 24 September 1955. In this amplitude–phase form the amplitude is 97.6 deaths per week and the peak falls at \(t = 2.67 \times 13/2\pi \approx 5.5\), around February 1956 (Figure 6.4). In R the same test is anova(m1, m2); models can also be compared by AIC (Pelat et al. 2007).






Figure 6.4: Reconstructed from Serfling (1963). (a) The baseline from Equation 6.2 and an illustrative epidemic threshold, set 1.64 times the weekly standard deviation (27.9 deaths) reported by Serfling above the baseline; in the original paper the standard deviation was also corrected for the extrapolated trend, so this gap widens over time. (b) The analysis of variance used to choose the number of harmonics. Hover panel (a) to read any period.

title: 6  Serfling
section: 6.4 Computing an epidemic threshold with Serfling
text:
6.4 Computing an epidemic threshold with Serfling
The four steps of Figure 6.1, in detail. Throughout, the aim is to separate ordinary baseline variation from what past epidemics left behind.

1. Clean the history. Remove or downweight past epidemics before fitting, so the baseline describes a year without them. Five ways are in use:

By calendar. Drop seasons or weeks known to be epidemic. Serfling used only non-epidemic seasons, replaced isolated high weeks with the trend value when estimating the spread, and, when many years in a row had epidemics, estimated the trend from the low season alone, roughly mid-May to mid-September (Serfling 1963). EuroMOMO fits only spring and autumn weeks, least affected by winter influenza and summer heat (EuroMOMO, n.d.).
By percentile. Drop a fixed share of the highest training weeks, typically about 15% (Pelat et al. 2007, 2017); on French influenza-like illness data the best configuration cut at the 86th percentile and used the full history (Souty et al. 2018).
Iteratively. Fit, drop the weeks above the fitted line and refit; then drop weeks above the upper 95% prediction limit and refit, until \(R^2\) stops increasing (Wang et al. 2015).
Robustly. Keep every week but fit by iteratively reweighted estimation, such as MASS::rlm, so unusual weeks lose weight on their own (Pelat et al. 2017). The CDC’s P&I baseline used a robust procedure (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 1998).
As censored. Treat each epidemic week as left-censored — without the epidemic it would have been at most what was observed — and mark weeks as epidemic one at a time, largest positive residual first, up to a set share (about 16% for acute respiratory infection) (Procházka and Kynčl 2016).



2. Fit and extrapolate. Estimate the coefficients on the cleaned data (by least squares, or a weighted or likelihood variant) and project \(\hat Y_t\) over the weeks to be monitored. That projection is the seasonal baseline, what to expect with no epidemic. Five years of training is common (EuroMOMO, n.d.; Pelat et al. 2017) but worth testing: on the French data the full history beat windows of 3, 5 or 10 years (Souty et al. 2018).


3. Set the threshold. Even with no epidemic the series scatters around the baseline, so the threshold sits a multiple of the forecast error above it:
\[ \text{Threshold}_t = \hat Y_t + z_\alpha\,\hat\sigma_t, \]
where \(\hat\sigma_t\), the standard deviation of the forecast error, combines the residual spread with the uncertainty of extrapolating. Serfling and the CDC use \(z = 1.64\)–\(1.645\) (Serfling 1963; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 1998); Serfling corrected for the extrapolated trend but not for the Fourier terms. This is the upper end of a one-sided 95% (or two-sided 90%) prediction interval, level = 0.90 in R’s predict() (McConeghy, n.d.). Santé publique France uses \(z \approx 1.96\), trading sensitivity for specificity (Pelat et al. 2017). On a log-normal model the threshold is \(\exp(\hat\mu_t + z_\alpha\hat\sigma)\), computed on the log scale (Procházka and Kynčl 2016).


4. Require two weeks. A single high week is as often a reporting delay or a data error as an epidemic. The onset is declared only when the series stays above the threshold two weeks in a row (Serfling 1963; Wang et al. 2015).


6.4.1 Working through the four steps
Step 1 decides the quality of the whole method: fit raw history and every past epidemic pulls the baseline up and swells the residual spread, so the threshold lands too high and new epidemics are flagged late (Unkel et al. 2012). Figure 6.5 simulates five training seasons, each with a winter epidemic, and a sixth to monitor. Because the data are simulated, the true baseline is known, and so is the real false alarm rate of any threshold. Choose a cleaning method, step through, then switch methods at any step to compare.






Figure 6.5: The four steps on simulated weekly data (season week 1 is July; noise standard deviation 10). Amber rings mark training weeks dropped or downweighted; the grey line is the true baseline, which the method never sees. All methods use \(z = 1.645\).

Untrimmed, the threshold barely fires and the epidemic is confirmed one week before its peak. Each cleaning method succeeds or fails for its own reason:

Calendar does best here because every epidemic falls inside the window (weeks 14–40, roughly October to March); it fails when one does not, and it leaves fewer weeks to fit.
Percentile is only as good as its share, which should be roughly the share of weeks actually epidemic: a quarter here, while the common 15% was tuned on French influenza-like illness (Souty et al. 2018). Trim 40% and the normal seasonal peak goes too; an ordinary week then crosses the threshold almost one time in five.
Iterative cleaning drops every week above the first fitted line, here 75 ordinary weeks with 45 epidemic ones, so the baseline ends about 10 too low in summer and 10 too high in winter, and \(s\) underestimates the noise.
Robust regression only reduces the weight of large residuals; with a quarter of the weeks epidemic, they still pull the baseline up. On the French data, too, it was less sensitive than periodic regression with trimming (Souty et al. 2018).

Cleaning also decides \(r\): untrimmed, the test for a second harmonic gives \(F = 27.8\), because the extra wave chases the epidemic peaks; at 15% trimming it falls to 1.6 (step 2 of the figure).


6.4.2 Why two weeks in a row
With \(z = 1.645\) an ordinary week still crosses the threshold about 5% of the time, two to three weeks a year (Serfling 1963). Over a 26-week winter–spring with no epidemic and independent weeks, the chance that at least one crosses is \(1 - 0.95^{26} = 0.736\). Two weeks in a row leaves 25 adjacent pairs, each crossing with probability \(0.05^2\), so the chance falls to at most \(25 \times 0.0025 = 0.0625\) — exactly 0.058; Serfling quoted about one in ten.
The price is time. The chance that a genuine rise is still unflagged after its second week is 0.9 for a moderate epidemic and 0.7 for a large one; after the third, 0.1 and under 0.01 (Serfling 1963). The arithmetic also assumes independent weeks; Serfling noted they are slightly correlated, and at a correlation of 0.4 the two-week false alarm rate triples, to about 17.5% (Figure 6.6).






Figure 6.6: Serfling’s argument, simulated. Each bar is one week of a 26-week season, in standard deviations from the baseline. Amber weeks cross the line alone; red weeks are confirmed by the week before. Simulate many seasons, then raise \(\rho\).





6.4.3 Excess burden
Once the epidemic period is identified, the model also estimates the excess burden, in one of two ways:

Against the baseline: \(\text{Excess}_t = Y_t - \hat{Y}_t\), summed over the epidemic weeks (Serfling 1963).
Against the threshold (more conservative): \(\text{Excess}_t = \max\left(Y_t - \text{Threshold}_t,\ 0\right)\), counting only the part above the threshold (McConeghy, n.d.).

title: 6  Serfling
text:
6.5 Variants and practical implementation

6.5.1 P&I mortality surveillance at the US CDC
The CDC applied Serfling to the percentage of all deaths due to pneumonia and influenza; a percentage is less biased than a count when the number of reporting units changes from week to week. The baseline came from periodic regression with a robust procedure, and the threshold was 1.645 standard deviations above it (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 1998). In October 2016 the data source moved from the 122 Cities Mortality Reporting System to the mortality surveillance system of the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2016).


6.5.2 Serfling–Poisson and EuroMOMO
Least squares assumes normal residuals with constant variance: reasonable for large counts, poor for small or sparse ones, or counts split by age group and small area (Unkel et al. 2012). The remedy is a generalised linear model (GLM) with a log link and a Poisson distribution corrected for overdispersion (quasi-Poisson):
\[
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \log\left(N_t\right) + \eta_0 + \eta_1 t + \eta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \eta_3\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right)
\]
where \(\mu_t\) is the expected count and \(\log\left(N_t\right)\) a population offset, included when population data exist so that the model estimates a rate.
This is the structure of EuroMOMO (European monitoring of excess mortality): a quasi-Poisson GLM with a linear trend and an annual sine wave, fitted on the spring and autumn weeks of up to five previous years, with a correction for delays in death registration (EuroMOMO, n.d.). FluMOMO adds influenza activity and extreme temperatures as explanatory variables (Nielsen et al. 2018); the modulation model lets the trend and the seasonal amplitude change smoothly over time through P-splines (Leger et al. 2025).

# df: weekly data with a column y (cases); the first 260 weeks are used for training
df$t  <- seq_len(nrow(df))
train <- df[df$t <= 260, ]
clean <- train[train$y <= quantile(train$y, 0.85), ]   # drop the highest 15% of weeks

m1 <- lm(y ~ t + cos(2*pi*t/52) + sin(2*pi*t/52), data = clean)
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + cos(4*pi*t/52) + sin(4*pi*t/52))

new$baseline  <- pred[, "fit"]
new$threshold <- pred[, "upr"]                          # baseline + 1.645 x forecast error
over          <- new$y > new$threshold
new$alarm     <- over & c(FALSE, head(over, -1))        # above the threshold 2 weeks running

title: 6  Serfling
text:
6.6 Comparison with other methods
Serfling works like a Shewhart control chart: each week is compared with the threshold on its own. That catches sudden surges well but is less sensitive to slow, smouldering rises (Unkel et al. 2012). This section compares it with three commonly used groups of methods.

6.6.1 The Moving Epidemic Method (MEM)
MEM, developed by Vega and colleagues for influenza surveillance in Europe (Vega et al. 2013), does not fit one wave to the whole year. It splits each past season into pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic periods using the maximum accumulated rate percentage (MAP) curve, and sets the threshold for a new season at the upper limit of a one-sided confidence interval of the highest pre-epidemic values. On influenza-like illness data from the French Sentinelles network, against an expert-consensus gold standard, Souty and colleagues found (Souty et al. 2018) (Figure 6.7):

Serfling (with percentile trimming) and MEM detected the epidemic start week equally well.
Serfling had higher specificity and positive predictive value; MEM had higher sensitivity.
Robust regression detected onsets less well and was the only method to split one epidemic season into two waves.







Figure 6.7: Performance of four methods in detecting influenza epidemics on French data (figures from Souty et al., 2018), each at its best detector. Choose a metric.





6.6.2 The Farrington algorithm
The Farrington algorithm (Farrington et al. 1996) and Noufaily’s improved version (Noufaily et al. 2013) are widely used in European routine surveillance and available in R’s surveillance package (Salmon et al. 2016). Farrington handles seasonality through its reference window: for week \(t_0\) it takes only the weeks within \(\pm w\) of the same time in the \(b\) previous years (for example \(w = 3\), \(b = 5\)) and fits a log-linear quasi-Poisson model:
\[
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 t,\qquad Var\left(y_t\right) = \phi\,\mu_t
\]
Past epidemics are downweighted by their residuals, and the threshold is computed after a 2/3 power transformation that makes even small counts close to normal:
\[
U_{t_0} = \hat{\mu}_{t_0}\left\{1 + \frac{2}{3}\, z_\alpha\,\frac{\left[\hat{\phi}\,\hat{\mu}_{t_0} + var\left(\hat{\mu}_{t_0}\right)\right]^{1/2}}{\hat{\mu}_{t_0}}\right\}^{3/2}
\]
With its quasi-Poisson structure and local window, Farrington suits low or sparse counts better than classical Serfling. It does not account for serial autocorrelation (Unkel et al. 2012).


6.6.3 The cumulative sum control chart (CUSUM)
CUSUM accumulates the positive standardised deviations over consecutive weeks:
\[
z_t = \frac{y_t - \mu_t}{\sigma_t},\qquad C_t = \max\left(0,\ C_{t-1} + z_t - k\right)
\]
and raises an alarm when \(C_t > h\), where \(k\) is the reference value and \(h\) the decision threshold (Unkel et al. 2012). Accumulating over many weeks, CUSUM is more sensitive than Serfling to small, sustained shifts. But it does not handle seasonality itself: without a baseline model to standardise the data (Serfling’s residuals, for example), it raises false alarms every time the peak season begins.

title: 6  Serfling
section: 6.7 Points to consider before applying it
text:
6.7 Points to consider before applying it
Serfling assumes a clear seasonality that repeats steadily from year to year, with a low period long enough to anchor the baseline (Unkel et al. 2012). That usually holds for influenza in temperate regions, with one winter peak a year, but not everywhere. Before applying the method to a disease, indicator or area, check four points.

A low period to anchor the baseline. If a disease circulates all year, cutting out calendar weeks loses its basis, and what remains may still hold epidemic activity. Feng and colleagues, estimating influenza-associated mortality in China, used Serfling only for northern cities with a clear winter peak; in the subtropical south influenza circulated all year (Feng et al. 2012).
The shape of the season. Several peaks, asymmetric peaks or patterns that differ between regions may need more than one harmonic, so test \(r\) on each area’s own data. In northern Vietnam influenza can peak several times a year, in different seasons (Horby et al. 2012), and its seasonality in Vietnam is weak overall (Servadio et al. 2023).
A stable peak timing. The model gives every year the same wave with a fixed phase. If the peak moves a lot between years, an average baseline fits no year well, and last year’s timing says little about next year’s. In Vietnam the interval between influenza peaks varies much more than in temperate regions (Servadio et al. 2023).
Performance in context. Figures such as the high specificity in the French study come from one disease, indicator and surveillance system and may not carry over. Re-evaluate the method on the historical series of the disease and area to be monitored before using it in operation.

title: 6  Serfling
text:
Summary

Serfling models the baseline as a long-term trend plus a Fourier series and sets the threshold about 1.645 standard deviations of the forecast error above it.
Each harmonic is a cosine–sine pair, equivalent to one wave with an amplitude and a phase. The analyst chooses \(r\) by testing; the data decide the coefficients.
Cleaning the history is the decisive step: left in, past epidemics push the threshold too high. Each cleaning method fails in its own way, so test it on the series to be monitored.
Requiring two consecutive weeks above the threshold reduces false alarms.
The Poisson variant (such as EuroMOMO) suits counts; Farrington and CUSUM complement Serfling when counts are small or an epidemic rises slowly.
In tropical regions, check the assumptions about seasonality first.
